solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Aptly, Evan withholds the odd request

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are held back, so only the even ones (second, fourth...) of these two words survive

parts.note: the letters are read straight from these two clue words

explanation.surface: Someone called Evan is fittingly reluctant to pass on a strange request.
explanation.walkthrough: Write out APTLYEVAN and drop letters 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; the even letters P, L, E, A remain.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea is an earnest appeal, a synonym for a request.

clue.text: RU sorted out with flea for this?

definitions.text: RU sorted out with flea for this?

indicators.note: things sorted out are rearranged, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rugby union body is dealt with by giving it a flea in the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: To send someone off with a flea in their ear is to scold them, and the scolding they get is an earful; RU is rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: An earful is a long angry telling-off, exactly what someone sent away with a flea in the ear receives.

clue.text: As expected, currently drone is flying

parts.note: currently means now, at present

indicators.note: something flying is moving about freely, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Predictably, a drone is up in the air at this very moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is flying' turns DRONE into WONDER, which follows NOW.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'no wonder' means it is unsurprising, i.e. just what one would have predicted.

clue.text: Zulu I found in this region

parts.note: Zulu is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for the letter Z
the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A Zulu person says they were discovered in this part of the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A zone is an area or district marked off from others, the same as a region.

clue.text: Flower close to garden behind

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like flower

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of garden

explanation.surface: A bloom grows near the garden, round the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is not a river here, just the bloom ASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is a nautical term for at or toward the back of a ship, so behind.

clue.text: Lens we're adapting for one once seen in cinemas

indicators.note: adapting something alters its form, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A camera operator explains they are modifying a lens for an old film screening.
explanation.definitionFit: Short filmed news bulletins were shown before the main feature in mid-century picture houses, a thing of the past.

clue.text: Help a son that's lost outside US city

indicators.note: the outside letters of the phrase are lost, so what remains is the run of letters held within it

parts.note: the letters sit inside these words, with H and N left over

explanation.surface: A plea to aid a boy who has gone missing outside a city in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' suggests an anagram, but it is the outside of HELPASON that is lost, leaving ELPASO.
explanation.definitionFit: El Paso is a city in western Texas on the Mexican border.

clue.text: Taking a chance, opens new clubs

indicators.note: a new version is a remade one, so these letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
C is the card-playing abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A gambler takes a risk and opens a fresh set of nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns OPENS into ONSPE, and C (clubs) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something 'on spec' means speculatively, without any guarantee of success, so as a gamble.

clue.text: Partially complete document initially coming in ninety minutes after noon?

indicators.note: one piece comes into another, so it is placed inside it

parts.note: ninety minutes past midday is half past one, written HALF ONE; the question mark flags the wordplay

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of document

explanation.surface: A report is half-finished, with the paperwork arriving at half past one.
explanation.walkthrough: Half one is the British way of saying half past one; D goes between HALF and ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something half-done is only partly finished, so incomplete to a degree.

clue.text: East London college as an alternative

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east
the LSE is the London School of Economics

explanation.surface: An East London college is offered as another option for study.
explanation.walkthrough: The London School of Economics is a famous college of the University of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Else means otherwise or instead, used to offer a different option, as in 'or else'.

clue.text: Volunteer troops one commanded followed

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, the British volunteer reserve force
the Roman numeral I is one
led means commanded or directed

explanation.surface: Reservists were tracked by a lone soldier who was in charge of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to shadow or track them closely, so tailed means pursued.

clue.text: A Liberal idea, incomplete, however

parts.note: L is the political abbreviation for Liberal

indicators.note: incomplete means the word is missing its last letter

parts.note: a thought is an idea

explanation.surface: A political party's half-formed notion, nevertheless, is put forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incomplete' removes the final T of THOUGHT, giving THOUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Although and however both introduce a concession, as in 'although it rained' versus 'however, it rained'.

clue.text: Info that is fabulous thing to get from bottle!

definitions.text: fabulous thing to get from bottle!

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A tip-off reveals that the marvellous prize in the bottle is waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fabulous' means belonging to fable or legend, not just excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend a spirit is released from a lamp or bottle and grants wishes, a mythical creature.

clue.text: Driver perhaps, to proceed left, following one in black suit

parts.note: go means to proceed or move along
f. is the abbreviation for following, used in page references
a club is a card from clubs, one of the two black suits

explanation.surface: A chauffeur is told to head off to the left after someone dressed in black.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' looks like a chauffeur but is the long-hitting wooden club in golf.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver is a specific example of a stick used in golf, the one for tee shots.

clue.text: English firm concerned with the environment

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A British company is said to care about green issues.
explanation.definitionFit: Eco is a prefix-style adjective meaning ecological, relating to nature and green issues.

clue.text: Something on a plate: it reflects to show wild animal

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a car's number plate shows its reg, short for registration
taken as written

explanation.surface: Food on a dish mirrors the image of a savage beast.
explanation.walkthrough: The plate is a vehicle number plate, not a dinner plate; REG and IT together are read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiger is a large striped big cat living in the wild, an example of a wild animal.

clue.text: US soldiers crossing desert, free

indicators.note: the soldiers cross over, straddling the other piece, so it ends up inside

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers
to rat is to desert or betray

explanation.surface: American troops travelling through the desert without charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' looks like a noun for sandy land but is the verb, RAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis is Latin-derived for without payment, costing nothing.

clue.text: Places for badges, round, almost 10

parts.note: a lap is a round of a circuit

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: refers to the answer at 10 across, which is the word else

explanation.surface: Pin-holders on a jacket circle back to an earlier clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of ELSE (the answer to 10 across), giving ELS after LAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Badges are commonly pinned on the folded flaps of a jacket's front, so they are spots that hold them.

clue.text: Father locks up a social outcast

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: A dad imprisons someone shunned by society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locks up' looks like imprisoning, but locks is HAIR and 'up' turns it around to RIAH after PA.
explanation.definitionFit: A pariah is a person rejected and avoided by others, a synonym for an outcast.

clue.text: Go off with a schedule

parts.note: to rot is to go off, decay

explanation.surface: Leave with a timetable in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is a list showing when each person takes their turn, a duty roster.

clue.text: Crook messed with ABM in secret planning location?

indicators.note: letters messed with are jumbled up, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A villain tampered with an anti-ballistic missile in a hidden war room.
explanation.walkthrough: ABM is an anti-ballistic missile; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Backroom deals are made out of public view, so a back room suggests a hidden place where schemes are hatched.

clue.text: Test version is live: much obliged!

parts.note: to be is to exist, to live
ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: A trial edition of software has gone live, and someone says thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A beta release is the preliminary edition of software given to users for trialling.

clue.text: Likelihood of fatal dose being taken by detective?

indicators.note: the first piece is taken by, held next to, the following one so it comes before it

parts.note: OD is an overdose, a fatal dose of a drug
DS is a detective sergeant

explanation.surface: A detective weighs the chances that a lethal dose was swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds express the probability of something happening, as in betting.

clue.text: Self-centred person, for example, first is after love

indicators.note: after places the last piece behind the one named before it

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
1st, written IST, is the abbreviation for first

explanation.surface: An egotist, for instance, puts themself first, ahead of love.
explanation.walkthrough: 1ST is read as the letters IST, as crosswords often treat the digit 1 as I.
explanation.definitionFit: An egoist puts their own interests above others, a selfish individual.

clue.text: Sheep and goose heard in African country

indicators.note: heard means the words are spoken aloud and the answer sounds like them

parts.note: a ewe is a female sheep and a gander a male goose; said together, ewe gander

explanation.surface: Farm animals are listened to in a nation of Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Said in a non-rhotic British accent, ewe-gander sounds like the country's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Uganda is a landlocked nation in East Africa.
